title: Mango Diplomacy: How a Seattle Tasting Event With Costco Signals India's Boldest Fruit Export Push Yet
excerpt: Seven premium varieties, 100 importers, a lieutenant governor, and Kesar mangoes selling out in two hours — the Indian mango's American moment has arrived.
body:
When the Indian Consulate in Seattle hosted the second edition of its "Mango Magic" festival on June 6, over 100 leading importers of Indian fruits gathered alongside senior representatives from Costco — a pairing that tells you everything about where Indian mangoes now sit in American retail.

Seven premium varieties were on display: Alphonso and Kesar from Maharashtra, Banganapalli and Himayat from Andhra Pradesh, Langra and Dussehri from Uttar Pradesh, and Rajapuri from Gujarat. A special Indian lunch featuring dishes made with each variety accompanied the tasting. By some accounts, stock of Kesar mangoes at local Costco stores sold out within two hours of hitting the shelves.

## From Ban to Bonanza

The arc of Indian mangoes in America begins with a simple diplomatic anecdote. In 2006, President George W. Bush visited India and tasted an Alphonso for the first time. "What a hell of a fruit," he reportedly told Prime Minister Manmohan Singh. The following year, after decades of a phytosanitary ban, Indian mangoes were finally cleared for import into the United States.

What started as a niche product for homesick NRIs has become a full-blown cultural phenomenon. Some importers now offer subscription "mango passes" costing up to $2,000 for weekly deliveries through the season. A single box of 10 to 12 Alphonso mangoes retails for $50 to $60, up from $40 to $45 last year.

"First, they mean very differently to Indian people," said Prakash Gupta, Consul General of India in Seattle. "It typically represents the onset of summer, and our growing-up memories are associated with this fruit. Families bond over mangoes."

## Washington State Gets on Board

The Seattle event was no small affair diplomatically. Washington State Lieutenant Governor Denny Heck attended and welcomed the growing presence of Indian mangoes in the US market. State Senators Tina Orwell, Manka Dhingra, and Vandana Slatter sampled the featured varieties. The Consuls General of Japan and Uzbekistan also showed up — turning a fruit tasting into a minor diplomatic gathering.

The event was organised in partnership with APEDA (Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority), India's agricultural export promotion body, signalling that mango exports are now a strategic priority for New Delhi, not just a seasonal trade.

Since the Consulate's first promotional event in Seattle on July 10, 2025, it has worked with stakeholders on both sides of the Pacific to get premium Indian mango varieties into major retail outlets. That Costco — headquartered just south of Seattle in Issaquah — is now a key distribution partner says as much about shifting American palates as it does about Indian agricultural diplomacy.

## The Diaspora Connection

For the millions of Indian Americans scattered across the country, mango season is the most emotionally loaded time of the culinary year. It is not about fruit. It is about the taste of childhood summers at grandparents' houses, of sticky fingers and steel plates, of a season that structured life in a way no American calendar marker ever could.

That emotional weight explains why NRIs will drive to warehouse pickup points at odd hours, track shipments on WhatsApp with the intensity of stock traders, and pay premium prices without hesitation. Every box that arrives in an American kitchen carries something money alone cannot quantify.

## What's Next

The Alphonso season typically tapers off by mid-June as the monsoon arrives in western India, with Kesar extending the window into early July. The industry is increasingly focused on GI certification, traceability, and building consumer trust around authenticated origin fruit. With Costco now stocking Indian mangoes in multiple regions and diplomatic efforts expanding to new cities, the question is no longer whether America will embrace the Indian mango. It is whether supply can ever keep up with demand.
